Ying Liu1∗
Yali Fu2

Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly equipped with
safety alignment mechanisms, yet recent studies demonstrate that
they remain vulnerable to jailbreaking attacks that elicit harmful be-
haviors without explicit policy violations. While a growing body of
work has explored automated jailbreak strategies, existing methods
face several fundamental challenges, including the lack of system-
atic utilization of both successful and failed attack experiences, as
well as the absence of principled mechanisms for composing and
selecting reusable attack rules under diverse constraints. As a result,
existing methods struggle to accumulate transferable knowledge
over time and to reliably adapt attack strategies across different
targets and evolving safety mechanisms. To address these issues,
we propose a Self-Evolving Rule-Driven Training-Free Jailbreak
(SRTJ) framework that systematically discovers, composes, and
refines attack strategies through interaction and feedback, without
updating model parameters. Specifically, SRTJ couples experience-
driven attack generation with answer set programming (ASP)-based
rule selection and constraint-aware composition, where iterative
verifier feedback is leveraged to jointly refine successful strategies
and analyze failure patterns. The resulting rule memory evolves in
a hierarchical multi-level manner, explicitly organizing distilled
attack knowledge into long-term, middle-term, and short-term
rules, thereby capturing both stable transferable strategies and
transient adaptive behaviors to effectively balance exploration and
exploitation across attack attempts. Extensive experiments on main-
stream jailbreak benchmark (HarmBench) demonstrate that SRTJ
achieves strong and stable attack performance across different tar-
get LLMs, while exhibiting improved robustness and generalization
compared to existing jailbreak methods. The code is available at
https://github.com/TheSolkatt/SRTJ.
1
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) [1, 2, 11, 17, 18, 38] have become a
core component of modern artificial intelligence, demonstrating
strong performance across a wide range of tasks such as natural
language understanding, reasoning, code generation, and question
answering. Owing to large-scale pretraining and instruction tuning,
LLMs are now widely deployed in both consumer-facing applica-
tions and high-stakes domains, serving as versatile foundations for
building intelligent systems.
Despite their impressive performance, LLMs also raise serious
safety and alignment concerns [16, 44, 45]. When exposed to ma-
licious or adversarial inputs, aligned models may still generate
harmful or policy-violating content, including instructions for ille-
gal activities, privacy breaches, or other misuse. To mitigate these
risks, modern LLMs are typically equipped with safety mechanisms
such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), safety
fine-tuning, and rule-based refusal policies. However, accumulating

The study of LLM jailbreaking [8, 26, 40, 45] has emerged as an
important research topic for systematically exposing vulnerabilities
of aligned language models under adversarial prompting, while
also serving as a practical tool for stress-testing and improving
safety mechanisms. Existing approaches mainly focus on attack
prompt generation and optimization, ranging from manually crafted
templates and role-playing strategies to automated, model-in-the-
loop methods that iteratively refine attacks based on target feedback,
including optimization-based attacks such as GCG [51], adaptive
prompt attacks such as AutoDAN [24], and agent-based frameworks
emphasizing automation and scalability.
Despite notable progress, existing jailbreak methods still face
fundamental challenges in effectively accumulating and exploiting
attack knowledge. (i) Lack of efficient and systematic utiliza-
tion of both successful and failed attack experiences. While
some prior work incorporates memory or history mechanisms,
these experiences are often stored in a naive or unstructured man-
ner, without distilling concise and reusable attack rules, leading
to inefficient reuse and limited long-term benefit. (ii) Absence of
principled mechanisms for composing and selecting reusable
attack rules under diverse constraints. Existing methods largely
rely on implicit prompt heuristics or ad hoc strategies, lacking
explicit and controllable procedures for selecting and composing
reusable attack rules that can adapt to varying attack goals, con-
straints, and target models. As a result, existing methods struggle
to accumulate transferable knowledge over time and to reliably
adapt attack strategies across different targets and evolving safety
mechanisms.

In this work, we propose SRTJ, a self-evolving, rule-driven, and
training-free jailbreak framework that systematically accumulates,
abstracts, and exploits attack experience over time. Instead of treat-
ing jailbreak prompts as isolated artifacts, SRTJ explicitly models
jailbreak as an experience-driven process, where successful attack
behaviors are progressively distilled into reusable symbolic rules.
To tackle challenge (i), SRTJ introduces a hierarchical, multi-
level memory to organize accumulated jailbreak experience. Rather
than storing raw attack prompts in a naive manner, SRTJ extracts
and consolidates successful attack patterns into concise and gen-
eralizable rules, which are selectively retained based on their ef-
fectiveness and success frequency. This design enables efficient
long-term reuse of high-quality attack strategies while preventing
uncontrolled memory growth and noise accumulation.
To overcome challenge (ii), SRTJ leverages answer set program-
ming (ASP) as a symbolic reasoning engine to perform explicit,
constraint-aware rule selection and composition. Given an attack
goal and contextual constraints, ASP systematically identifies com-
patible rules and assembles them into valid attack strategies, of-
fering stronger controllability and compositional reliability than
purely language-based reasoning. By decoupling symbolic strategy
planning from natural language realization, SRTJ remains robust
to prompt surface variations and adaptable to diverse target LLMs.
During deployment, SRTJ iteratively refines its rule repository
based on accumulated attack outcomes, enabling progressively
more effective rule composition without any model training. This
process leads to strong and stable attack performance across dif-
ferent target LLMs, as illustrated in Fig. 1 for both single-turn and
multi-turn settings.
Our contributions can be summarized as follows:
• We propose SRTJ, a novel training-free jailbreak framework
that formulates LLM jailbreaking as a self-evolving, rule-
driven process, enabling systematic discovery and reuse of
attack strategies without model fine-tuning.
• We introduce an experience accumulation and rule evolution
mechanism that integrates symbolic rule composition with
LLM-based attack generation, allowing effective knowledge
consolidation across jailbreak attempts.
• We conduct extensive experiments on the mainstream jail-
break benchmark (HarmBench) and target LLMs, demon-
strating that SRTJ achieves strong and stable attack perfor-
mance with improved robustness and generalization com-
pared to existing methods.
2
Related Work
2.1
LLM Jailbreaking
2.1.1
Single-turn Attacks. Single-turn methods aim to bypass
the safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) using a
single prompt, without iterative interaction or multi-round feed-
back. These methods typically operate at the prompt level and ex-
ploit weaknesses in safety generalization through one-shot or non-
interactive attacks. A line of work focuses on adversarial prompt
optimization. GCG [51] proposes a greedy coordinate gradient
method to construct universal adversarial suffixes that induce harm-
ful responses when appended to benign queries. PAIR [6] studies
a black-box setting where an attacker LLM automatically refines
prompts based on model feedback, showing that effective jailbreak
prompts can be discovered with a small number of queries. Other ap-
proaches emphasize semantic and natural-language-based prompt
manipulation. AutoDAN [24] uses a hierarchical genetic algorithm
to generate fluent and semantically meaningful jailbreak prompts,
demonstrating improved stealthiness against perplexity-based de-
fenses. PAP [47] investigates persuasion-based attacks, showing
that human-like conversational framing can elicit unsafe responses
from aligned models. Several works explore representation shifts
that expose safety generalization gaps. Multilingual jailbreaks [9] re-
veal that safety alignment trained on high-resource languages may
not generalize well to other languages. CipherChat [46] encodes
inputs using ciphers, leading to increased harmful behaviors under
encoded prompts. CodeAttack [31] reformulates harmful queries
as code completion tasks, demonstrating that safety mechanisms
trained on natural language may fail to generalize to code-based
inputs. ReNeLLM [10] further shows that nested and compositional
prompt structures can induce jailbreaks within a single forward
pass.
2.1.2
Multi-turn Attacks. Multi-turn jailbreaking attacks exploit
the conversational nature of large language models (LLMs) by dis-
tributing malicious intent across multiple interaction rounds, rather
than issuing a single explicit harmful query. By leveraging dia-
logue history, contextual accumulation, and intermediate model
responses, these methods aim to bypass safety mechanisms that are
primarily optimized for single-turn inputs. A line of work adopts
role-playing or hypothetical scenarios to guide models toward un-
safe behaviors over multiple turns. Red Queen [19] shows that
LLMs can be induced to generate harmful outputs when prompts
are framed as fictional settings or assigned roles (e.g., “You are
a role ...”), revealing latent multi-turn safety risks that do not
manifest under isolated queries. Similarly, CFA [37] studies multi-
turn semantic jailbreaks and proposes a context fusion strategy
that constructs contextual scenarios around a target query, dynam-
ically integrating and replacing malicious keywords to conceal
direct harmful intent while preserving semantic relevance. Other
approaches rely on fixed communication patterns or progressive
escalation strategies. Crescendo [33] facilitates benign interactions
across multiple turns and incrementally steers the model toward un-
safe behaviors by referencing its own previous responses. CoA [41]
frames multi-turn jailbreaking as an interrogation process, adap-
tively generating attack chains based on dialogue history and se-
mantic feedback to gradually expose harmful capabilities. More re-
cently, ActorBreaker [32] investigates multi-turn jailbreaks through
natural distribution shifts, constructing attack trajectories that ex-
ploit semantic relationships between benign and toxic concepts. By
modeling interactions among different actors in a dialogue, Actor-
Breaker demonstrates that aligned LLMs may exhibit safety gaps
under naturally evolving multi-turn conversations.

reuse information beyond a single forward pass, enabling models
to maintain state, improve consistency, and support long-horizon
interaction. A canonical paradigm is retrieval-augmented gener-

3
Methodology
In this section, we present SRTJ, a self-evolving, rule-driven, and
training-free framework for LLM jailbreaking. Unlike prior ap-
proaches that rely on handcrafted prompt templates or model fine-
tuning, SRTJ explicitly models jailbreak attacks as a structured, se-
quential process that accumulates experience and evolves reusable
strategies over time. The core design principle of SRTJ is to de-
couple symbolic decision making from natural language realization,
enabling systematic strategy search under black-box access and
limited query budgets. An overview of our framework is illustrated
in Fig. 2. The end-to-end execution of SRTJ is formally specified
in Algorithm 1, which details the iterative interaction among at-
tack generation, verifier feedback, and experience evolution. (More
Details are in Appendix B)

3.2
Self-Evolving Jailbreak as a Sequential
Decision Process
We model the jailbreak process as a sequential decision process
with an explicitly evolving internal state. At iteration 𝑡, the system
state is defined as
X𝑡= (R𝑡, E𝑡),

tion. This design allows SRTJ to operate entirely in a training-free
manner while still exhibiting adaptive behavior over time.
3.3
Rule Representation and Symbolic
Abstraction
A central component of SRTJ is the use of symbolic rules to repre-
sent reusable jailbreak experience. Each rule 𝜌∈R is defined as a
structured abstraction
𝜌= (𝑢, Φ, z,𝜔),
(8)
where𝑢is a natural language description of the underlying strategy,
Φ = {𝜙𝑘} is a set of symbolic predicates, z denotes associated se-
mantic tags, and 𝜔stores statistical attributes such as usage counts
and success rates.
The predicate set Φ is drawn from a predefined ontology and cap-
tures high-level strategy properties, including persuasion strategy,
linguistic tone, formatting style, and structural constraints. By de-
sign, predicates are domain-agnostic and don’t encode goal-specific
operational details. This abstraction enables rules to be reused
across different goals while remaining compatible with symbolic
reasoning. Detailed roles of symbolic reasoning are in Appendix B.1.
Crucially, rules represent strategic intent rather than concrete
prompt realizations. This separation allows SRTJ to reason over
strategies at a symbolic level while delegating surface-level lan-
guage generation to a separate instantiation module.
3.4
Rule-Guided Attack Generation via Answer
Set Programming (ASP)
Attack generation in SRTJ proceeds through a two-stage process
that decouples symbolic strategy selection from natural language
realization, where ASP enables constraint-aware strategy selection
over evolving jailbreak rules. Definition and more details of ASP
are in Appendix B.2.
Exploratory generation. When the rule library is empty or in-
sufficient, i.e., R𝑡= ∅, the system performs exploratory attack gen-
eration. In this mode, prompts are generated directly by a language
model to probe the target model’s safety mechanisms. Exploratory
attempts are strictly bounded to control query cost and serve as
the primary source of initial experience for rule discovery. This
bounded exploratory attack loop, which is used for cold-start ex-
ploration and as a fallback when rule-guided generation becomes
ineffective, is formally specified in Algorithm 2 (Appendix B.3).
Rule-guided generation. Once reusable rules have been accu-
mulated, SRTJ switches to rule-guided attack generation. Given
the current rule library R𝑡, accumulated experience E𝑡−1, and goal
𝑔, the system solves a symbolic rule selection problem:
𝜋𝑡∈ASP-Solve(R𝑡,𝑔, E𝑡−1),
(9)
where 𝜋𝑡⊆R𝑡denotes a compatible set of rules.
The ASP formulation encodes rule applicability conditions, mu-
tual exclusion constraints, coverage requirements, and prohibitions
against previously failed rule combinations. By explicitly modeling
these constraints, SRTJ can systematically explore the combinato-
rial space of constraint-aware strategy compositions while avoiding
invalid or redundant attempts.
After selecting a rule set 𝜋𝑡, a language model instantiates the
symbolic strategies into a concrete prompt
𝑝𝑡∼G(𝑔, 𝜋𝑡),

3.5
Verifier-Guided Feedback Signal
The verifier plays a critical role in enabling self-evolution with-
out model training. Our design is conceptually inspired by recent
training-free optimization paradigms, particularly Training-Free
GRPO [5, 34], which leverage external feedback to guide behavior
without updating model parameters. Unlike GRPO-style methods
that perform policy optimization, the verifier in SRTJ serves purely
as an internal feedback oracle, providing signals for experience
accumulation and rule evolution rather than model learning.
For each response 𝑟𝑡, the verifier returns a scalar score 𝑠𝑡and,
when applicable, a textual failure analysis 𝑓𝑡. The binary success
indicator 𝑦𝑡= I(𝑠𝑡≥𝜏) provides a unified supervision signal for
downstream modules.
Unlike external evaluation metrics, the verifier is used exclu-
sively as an internal feedback oracle. Its outputs guide experience
accumulation, rule harvesting, and credit assignment, but don’t
directly determine final performance reporting. Failure analyses
are retained and incorporated into subsequent attack generation to
discourage repeated failure while preserving symbolic constraints.

Hierarchical Memory

Why symbolic rules instead of prompt templates? While
prompt templates provide a convenient way to express attacks, they
are inherently tied to surface-level linguistic realizations and tend
to generalize poorly across goals and contexts. SRTJ instead adopts
symbolic rules as a higher-level abstraction of jailbreak experience,
capturing reusable strategy patterns that are decoupled from spe-
cific prompt phrasings. This abstraction supports principled rule
composition, systematic exploration under constraints, and efficient
reuse of distilled attack knowledge, avoiding repeated rediscovery
of similar behaviors.
Why verifier-based feedback? Rather than relying on hand-
crafted heuristics or direct prompt optimization, SRTJ employs a
verifier as an internal feedback signal to guide experience accu-
mulation and rule evolution. The verifier provides coarse-grained
success indicators and auxiliary failure information that inform
subsequent attack generation, without performing model learn-
ing or serving as a final evaluation metric. This design enables
iterative refinement of attack strategies while preserving a training-
free paradigm and maintaining a clear separation between attack
generation and evaluation.

Conclusion
In this paper, we proposed SRTJ, a self-evolving, rule-driven, and
training-free framework for LLM jailbreaking. By reframing jail-
break attacks as a process of efficient experience utilization and
principled rule composition, SRTJ enables systematic discovery,
abstraction, and reuse of effective attack strategies without relying
on model training or handcrafted prompt heuristics. Leveraging
concise multi-level experiences distilled from successful attacks
and constraint-aware rule selection via answer set programming
(ASP), SRTJ demonstrates strong and stable attack performance
on the HarmBench benchmark across both proprietary and open-
source target LLMs. More broadly, our findings suggest that elevat-
ing jailbreaking from prompt-level optimization to strategy-level
experience evolution offers a promising direction for scalable, trans-
ferable, and interpretable evaluation of LLM safety mechanisms.

Additional Related Work
A.1
Formalization or Logic-Based Approaches
Recent surveys have highlighted the growing role of logical rea-
soning and neuro-symbolic frameworks in improving the reason-
ing robustness, controllability, and safety of large language mod-
els [4, 7, 23, 42]. These studies systematically review how formal
logic, symbolic representations, and rule-based reasoning can com-
plement neural language models and expose limitations of purely
data-driven approaches. Building on this line of work, several re-
cent studies have explored symbolic and logic-based formulations
in the context of LLM safety and jailbreaking. LogiBreak [30] for-
mulates malicious intents using formal logical expressions and
exploits logical equivalence and transformation rules to bypass
safety constraints, demonstrating that aligned models remain vul-
nerable to semantically equivalent but structurally transformed
logical inputs. MathPrompt [3] encodes harmful prompts into sym-
bolic mathematics problems using set theory, abstract algebra, and
symbolic logic, revealing that safety mechanisms trained on natu-
ral language inputs fail to generalize to mathematically encoded
representations. Beyond jailbreak-specific settings, symbolic rea-
soning has also been explored through rule-based representations.
RuleGenie [36] leverages large language models to analyze, com-
pare, and optimize symbolic rule sets under explicit logical and
performance constraints, illustrating how LLMs can be integrated
with structured rule systems for reasoning over complex symbolic
programs.
Overall, existing jailbreak methods mainly focus on prompt-level
manipulation or interaction strategies under specific attack settings.
As a result, attack attempts are often treated as isolated processes,
and successful experiences are rarely abstracted into reusable and
transferable knowledge. In parallel, prior research on LLM memory
primarily targets general agent behavior, long-horizon interaction,
or self-improvement, with limited exploration in adversarial attack
generation. These limitations suggest the need for mechanisms
that can systematically accumulate, organize, and exploit attack
experience over time.
B
Additional Methodology
B.1
Symbolic Reasoning
Symbolic reasoning provides a formal mechanism for representing
structured knowledge and enforcing logical constraints through
explicit rules. In contrast to purely neural approaches that rely on
implicit pattern learning, symbolic methods enable interpretable,
compositional, and constraint-aware reasoning, which is particu-
larly suitable for tasks involving rule selection, compatibility check-
ing, and strategy composition. Specifically, this work utilizes the
Answer Set Programming (ASP) system and symbolic reasoning to
abstract and organize jailbreak strategies at the rule level, enabling
structured reuse and controlled composition across different attack
goals and categories.
B.1.1
Answer Set Programming (ASP). Answer Set Program-
ming (ASP) is a declarative logic programming paradigm designed
for solving combinatorial search and constraint satisfaction prob-
lems. ASP programs consist of a set of logical rules and constraints,
whose computed solutions, named answer sets, represent stable and
self-consistent models that satisfy all specified conditions.
An ASP program is typically composed of several basic syntactic
elements: Atoms are the basis of the ASP program and specify the
most fundamental semantic units, representing the propositions
that can be either true or false; Facts specify unconditional truths;
Rules define logical dependencies between atoms and enable the
derivation of new conclusions under specified conditions; Con-
straints are used to prohibit undesired combinations of atoms and
encode compatibility or applicability restrictions; Choice rules allow
the ASP to select arbitrary subsets of atoms from a given domain,
supporting flexible combination and selection behaviors.
Formally, the ASP program is defined over a set of atoms and
typically includes rules of the form:
𝑎:- 𝑏1, . . . ,𝑏𝑚, not 𝑐1, . . . , not 𝑐𝑛,
(14)
where 𝑎, 𝑏𝑖, and 𝑐𝑗are atoms, and not denotes default negation.
Constraints can be expressed by the above rules with empty heads,
which eliminate invalid combinations of atoms from admissible
answer sets.
In the context of our SRTJ, ASP serves as a symbolic abstrac-
tion mechanism for rule composition. High-level jailbreak rules
are treated as symbolic units, and ASP-style constraints are used
to enforce compatibility, applicability, and structural consistency
when composing multiple rules into a unified attack strategy. By
decoupling symbolic strategy selection from surface-level prompt
realization, this symbolic formulation facilitates modular reuse
of jailbreak knowledge while preserving flexibility in natural lan-
guage generation. Moreover, the non-monotonic nature of ASP
offers a conceptual foundation for modeling the evolving validity
of jailbreak rules where newly accumulated experience or failure
feedback may invalidate previously effective strategy combinations.
